headings.title: Introduction to Nutrition in HIV Management
headings.content: Nutrition plays a vital role in the comprehensive care of people living with HIV. Good food acts as both support for the immune system and a partner to antiretroviral therapy. When a person is well-nourished, their body can better handle the demands of the virus and the medicines used to fight it. Conversely, poor nutrition speeds up disease progression, weakens the body's natural defenses, and makes side effects from drugs harder to bear. For nursing students, understanding this link means seeing food not just as comfort, but as an active part of clinical care.

headings.title: Nutritional Goals and Requirements
headings.content:
Energy and nutrient needs shift as HIV progresses through its stages. An asymptomatic person needs slightly more energy than someone without HIV, while an actively ill or symptomatic patient requires a significant increase in calories and protein to prevent wasting. 

- **Energy intake**: Increase daily calories by 10 percent during asymptomatic stages and up to 30 percent during symptomatic or weight-loss phases.
- **Protein requirements**: Higher amounts are necessary to maintain and repair lean body mass, especially during infections or recovery periods.
- **Fluid balance**: Essential for supporting metabolic processes and helping the kidneys clear medication byproducts.

headings.title: Macronutrient and Micronutrient Management
headings.content: Micronutrient deficiencies are common in HIV due to poor intake, malabsorption, and chronic inflammation. Vitamins A, C, E, and B-complex, along with minerals like zinc and selenium, play crucial roles in maintaining immune cell function and reducing oxidative stress. However, nurses must advise caution with high-dose single-nutrient supplements, as excessive intake can sometimes cause toxicity or worsen viral replication. Whole foods remain the safest and most effective vehicle for these essential vitamins and minerals.

headings.title: Nutritional Assessment and Monitoring
headings.content:
Regular nutritional screening catches subtle declines before they turn into severe wasting. The nursing assessment involves tracking body weight trends, calculating body mass index, and asking about dietary changes or swallowing difficulties. 

| Assessment Tool | Clinical Purpose | Nursing Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Weight Tracking | Identifies sudden or gradual loss | Weigh patient at every clinic visit |
| Dietary Recall | Evaluates actual food and fluid intake | Ask what the patient ate in the last 24 hours |
| Physical Exam | Checks for muscle wasting or pallor | Inspect skin, hair, mouth, and extremities |

Spotting early signs of lipodystrophy or nutrient deficits allows the care team to intervene quickly.

headings.title: Managing HIV-Related Symptoms and Metabolic Complications
headings.content: Gastrointestinal symptoms like nausea, diarrhea, and oral thrush make eating a daily struggle. Nurses help patients manage these barriers by suggesting small, frequent meals, bland foods, and good oral hygiene. Beyond immediate symptoms, long-term antiretroviral therapy can lead to metabolic changes such as dyslipidemia and insulin resistance. Dietary adjustments, including reducing saturated fats and increasing fiber, help protect cardiovascular health in aging populations living with HIV.

headings.title: Drug-Nutrient Interactions
headings.content: Food can change how the body absorbs antiretroviral medications, and medicines can alter how the body handles nutrients. Some drugs must be taken on an empty stomach to ensure proper absorption, while others require food to reduce severe stomach irritation or enhance uptake. Nurses must review timing instructions carefully with patients. A common misconception is that all supplements are safe to take alongside prescription drugs; in reality, certain herbal products can dangerously lower drug levels in the blood.

headings.title: Food Safety, Hygiene, and Water Sanitation
headings.content: Because an immunocompromised body struggles to fight off foodborne pathogens, food safety is a critical pillar of HIV care. Unsafe water and poorly handled food can lead to severe, prolonged diarrhea, which rapidly worsens malnutrition. Nurses must teach basic hygiene practices: washing hands before eating or preparing meals, washing fruits and vegetables thoroughly, cooking meats completely, and boiling drinking water when safety is uncertain.

headings.title: Counseling and Support Strategies for Nurses
headings.content: Nutritional counseling must be practical, culturally sensitive, and realistic for the patient's economic situation. Telling a patient to eat expensive imported foods is unhelpful when local resources can provide the exact same nutrients. Nurses should explore affordable local food options, involve family members in education when appropriate, and address food insecurity by connecting patients with community support programs. Compassionate guidance helps patients maintain their health and dignity over the long term.
